'''''Abies nordmanniana''''', the '''Nordmann fir''' or '''Caucasian fir''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a [[fir]] [[Indigenous (ecology)|indigenous]] to the [[mountain]]s south and east of the [[Black Sea]], in [[Turkey]], [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] and the [[Russia]]n [[Caucasus]]. It occurs at elevations of 900–2,200 m on mountains with precipitation of over 1,000 mm.

The current distribution of the Nordmann fir is associated with the [[forest]] [[refugium (population biology)|refugia]] that existed during the [[Last Glacial Period|Ice Age]] at the eastern and southern [[Black Sea]] coast. In spite of currently suitable [[climate]], the species is not found in areas of the Eastern [[Greater Caucasus]], which are separated from the Black Sea Coast by more than 400–500 km.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors =Tarkhnishvili D, Gavashelishvili A, Mumladze L |title=Palaeoclimatic models help to understand current distribution of Caucasian forest species |journal=Biol. J. Linn. Soc. |volume = 105|issue=105 |pages=231–248 |date=2012 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8312.2011.01788.x|doi-access=free }}</ref>
[[File:Hortus Haren (Groningen) 13-12-2025. (actm.) 11.jpg|thumb|255px|Typical rootstock of a ''Abies nordmanniana''. (Nordmann fir.)]]

== Description ==
It is a large [[evergreen]] [[conifer]]ous [[tree]] growing to 55–61 m tall and with a [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] [[diameter]] of up to 2 m. In the [[Western Caucasus]] Reserve, some specimens have been reported to be {{convert|78|m|ft|abbr=on}} and even {{convert|85|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall,<ref>{{cite web | url = https://whc.unesco.org/archive/advisory_body_evaluation/900.pdf | title = Western Caucasus WHA, IUCN Technical Evaluation}}</ref> the tallest [[tree]]s in the [[Caucasus]], [[Anatolia]], the [[Russia|Russian Federation]] and the [[Europe|continent of Europe]].{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

The [[leaf|leaves]] are needle-like, flattened, 1.8–3.5 cm long and 2 mm wide by 0.5 mm thick, glossy dark green above, and with two blue-white bands of [[stomata]] below. The tip of the leaf is usually blunt, often slightly notched at the tip, but can be pointed, particularly on strong-growing shoots on young trees. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are 10–20 cm long and 4–5 cm broad, with about 150–200 scales, each scale with an exserted bract and two winged [[seed]]s; they disintegrate when mature to release the seeds.

==Taxonomy==

The species is named by [[Christian von Steven]] after his compatriot, the Finnish zoologist [[Alexander von Nordmann]] (1803–1866), who was the director of the [[Odessa Botanical Garden]]s.

===Subspecies===
There are two subspecies (treated as distinct species by some botanists), intergrading where they meet in northern [[Turkey]] at about 36°E longitude:
* Caucasian fir (''Abies nordmanniana'' subsp. ''nordmanniana''). Native to the [[Caucasus (mountains)|Caucasus]] mountains and eastern [[Pontic Mountains]] of northeastern Turkey west to about 36°E. Shoots often pubescent (hairy).
* Turkish fir ([[Abies nordmanniana subsp. equi-trojani|''Abies nordmanniana'' subsp. ''equi-trojani'']]). Native to northwestern Turkey, including the western Pontic Mountains as well as [[Uludağ]] and other mountains southeast of the [[Sea of Marmara]]. Often treated as a separate species, ''Abies bornmuelleriana''.<ref name = conifer>Kaya, Zeki, A. Skaggs, David Brian Neale (2008). "Genetic Differentiation of Abies equi-trojani (Asch. & Sint. ex Boiss) Mattf. Populations from Kazdağı, Turkey and the Genetic Relationship between Turkish Firs belonging to the Abies nordmanniana Spach Complex". ''Turkish Journal of Botany'' 32 (2008) 1-10</ref> In Turkey this subspecies is treated as a distinct species (''Abies equi-trojani'' <small>Asch. & Sint. ex Bois.</small>). It is endemic to a single location on [[Mount Ida (Turkey)|Kaz Dağı]] (Mount Ida) in [[Balıkesir Province]], northwestern [[Turkey]].<ref name="Alizoti-2009">{{Cite journal|last1=Alizoti|first1=P.G.|last2=Fady|first2=B.|last3=Prada|first3=M.A.|last4=Vendramin|first4=G.G|year=2009|title=Mediterranean firs - ''Abies spp.''|url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin//templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Technical_guidelines/1507_Mediterranen_firs_Abies_spp.pdf|journal=EUFORGEN Technical Guidelines for Genetic Conservation and Use|access-date=2016-10-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161020035525/http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin//templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Technical_guidelines/1507_Mediterranen_firs_Abies_spp.pdf|archive-date=2016-10-20}}</ref> This subspecies occupies an area of only 164 km<sup>2</sup> and is assessed as "Endangered".<ref>{{cite iucn |author=Knees, S. |author2=Gardner, M. |date=2011 |title=''Abies nordmanniana'' subsp. ''equi-trojani'' |volume=2011 |article-number=e.T31325A9626365 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2011-2.RLTS.T31325A9626365.en |access-date=19 November 2021}}</ref> Its shoots are usually glabrous (hairless).<ref name = conifer/>

== Cultivation and uses ==
The Nordmann fir is one of the most important species grown for [[Christmas tree]]s, being favoured for its attractive foliage, with needles that are not sharp and do not drop readily when the tree dries out.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

It is also a popular ornamental tree in [[park]]s and large [[garden]]s, and along with the [[cultivar]] 'Golden Spreader'<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=2073 |title=RHS Plant Selector Abies nordmanniana 'Golden Spreader' AGM / RHS Gardening |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |access-date=2013-11-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131105182710/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=2073 |archive-date=2013-11-05 }}</ref> has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=7 |title=RHS Plant Selector Abies nordmanniana AGM / RHS Gardening |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |access-date=2013-11-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131105183301/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=7 |archive-date=2013-11-05 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 1 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 14 August 2019}}</ref>

In Europe, the tree has also been used for reforestation as a way to mitigate expected forest decline caused by climate changes.<ref name="Alizoti-2009" />

The [[wood]] is soft and white, and is used for general construction, [[paper]], etc.
